title: Demand or supply-driven? How firms view inflation right now
gist: ECB staff use earnings-call/press textual analysis and business-survey structural models to show the euro area's 2026 inflation surge (1.9%→2.8% YoY, Feb-June) triggered by the Middle East war is overwhelmingly a supply/cost-push shock centered on energy-intensive manufacturing, and is materially milder and less demand-driven than the 2022 post-Ukraine-invasion episode.

themes.theme: The Middle East war reignites an energy-driven inflation shock

insights.claim: Euro area headline inflation rose from 1.9% to 2.8% year on year between February and June 2026, driven by a crude oil price surge triggered by the war in the Middle East.
insights.speaker: ECB Blog
insights.so_what: A ~90bp inflation jump concentrated in energy gives a concrete magnitude for gauging how much of current euro area inflation is a one-off supply shock versus something the ECB needs to actively fight.
insights.quote: the surge in crude oil prices triggered by the conflict led to a sharp upswing in energy inflation, pushing euro area headline inflation up from 1.9% to 2.8% year on year
insights.locator: The war in the Middle East has brought this challenge back to the fore.

insights.claim: The authors judge the 2026 inflation surge to be largely an energy supply shock, structurally reminiscent of the shock following Russia's February 2022 invasion of Ukraine, though the underlying demand/supply balance at each shock's onset differs.
insights.speaker: ECB Blog
insights.so_what: Investors comparing this episode to 2022 should note the authors explicitly flag that shock type alone isn't enough — the demand/supply balance and shock persistence at onset also shape the appropriate policy response.
insights.locator: Now as then, the inflation surge appears to be largely driven by an energy supply shock.

insights.claim: Demand-pull inflation calls for a firm central bank policy response, while supply-driven (cost-push) inflation warrants a more careful assessment because it is often driven by factors outside a central bank's control and should be weathered rather than fought.
insights.speaker: ECB Blog
insights.so_what: This is the interpretive lens the ECB itself uses to decide whether to tighten aggressively or hold — useful for anticipating ECB reaction functions to future supply shocks (e.g. further oil spikes).
insights.quote: Demand-driven inflation (sometimes called demand-pull inflation) calls for a firm policy response. Meanwhile, supply-driven inflation (also known as cost-push inflation) warrants a more careful assessment.
insights.locator: For central banks, whether inflation stems from demand or supply makes a crucial difference.

themes.theme: Real-time signals from earnings calls and financial press

insights.claim: In May 2026, firms' attention to inflation and inflation risk in earnings calls had intensified since the Middle East conflict began, but remained below the levels and volatility observed in March 2022 after Russia's invasion of Ukraine.
insights.speaker: ECB Blog
insights.so_what: Corporate management commentary is signaling that firms themselves view the current shock as less severe than 2022 — a leading indicator investors can track via earnings-call transcripts before hard inflation data confirms it.
insights.locator: A first clue comes from earnings calls

insights.claim: A causality-extraction text analysis of Financial Times articles shows that since the Middle East war began, supply-side narratives (energy costs, supply chain disruption) have dominated inflation coverage far more than demand-side narratives (consumer spending, monetary stimulus), a starker skew toward supply-push framing than in 2022 when narratives were more balanced and supply-chain-disruption stories were more prominent.
insights.speaker: ECB Blog
insights.so_what: Press-narrative concentration on energy costs (rather than broad supply-chain or demand stories) is an early, non-official signal pointing to a narrower, more clearly cost-push inflation episode than 2022.
insights.quote: since the start of the war in the Middle East demand-side narratives ... have played a smaller role than supply narratives ... In contrast, there was a broader mix of narratives back in 2022

insights.claim: The authors treat earnings-call textual analysis and press causality-extraction as timely, forward-looking indicators specifically because they are available well ahead of official hard inflation and survey data, making them useful for real-time monetary policy assessment.
insights.speaker: ECB Blog
insights.so_what: This is a reusable methodology (NLP on earnings calls plus causal text-mining of financial press) that investors and analysts can replicate to get an early read on demand-vs-supply inflation framing ahead of ECB or Eurostat releases.
insights.locator: Crucially, both approaches are based on timely, forward-looking indicators.

themes.theme: Business-survey structural decomposition points to a narrow, energy-linked supply shock

insights.claim: A monthly Bayesian structural VAR on European Commission business surveys shows the composite index of business price expectations rose markedly after the Middle East war broke out mainly because of cost-push shocks, while demand-pull pressures stayed broadly stable.
insights.speaker: ECB Blog
insights.so_what: A structural model attributing the entire rise in price expectations to supply rather than demand strengthens the case that the ECB does not need to treat this shock like a demand-driven overheating episode.
insights.locator: The composite index of business price expectations rose markedly after the outbreak of the war in the Middle East

insights.claim: A more granular quarterly model shows the 2026 supply shock is driven mainly by materials-supply shortages linked to higher energy prices, and is concentrated in energy-intensive manufacturing subsectors such as chemicals, refined petroleum and paper products.
insights.speaker: ECB Blog
insights.so_what: Investors in energy-intensive industrials (chemicals, refining, paper) should expect the most direct and visible margin pressure from this shock, while services and construction cost expectations should be comparatively less disturbed at the source.
insights.quote: these shocks mainly reflected materials supply shortages – linked to higher energy prices – and were concentrated in manufacturing – particularly in energy-intensive subsectors such as chemicals, refined petroleum and paper products
insights.locator: At granular level, these shocks mainly reflected materials supply shortages

insights.claim: The composite business price expectations index is a gross-value-added-weighted average across sectors with services weighted at 71%, manufacturing at 22% and construction at 7%, so a manufacturing-concentrated energy shock still moves the aggregate reading materially via cost pass-through.
insights.speaker: ECB Blog
insights.so_what: Because services dominate the composite index's weighting, any spread of energy cost pass-through from manufacturing into services pricing would be the key signal to watch for broadening inflation risk.
insights.locator: Composite business price expectations refer to the gross value added-weighted average

insights.claim: The quarterly structural model separates six shock types — three demand-side (product demand, financial conditions, other demand) and three supply-side (materials supply, labour conditions, other supply) — giving a granular attribution framework for what is moving firms' price and activity expectations.
insights.speaker: ECB Blog
insights.so_what: This six-factor decomposition is a reusable diagnostic template for tracking whether future price pressure comes from labour costs, financing conditions, or materials/energy shortages specifically.
insights.locator: A more granular quarterly model can then help us to further tease out factor-specific drivers

themes.theme: 2026 versus 2022: a materially milder, narrower shock

insights.claim: Business price expectations after Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine stood roughly two standard deviations above their current (2026) level, indicating the 2022 inflationary shock was far broader-based and more intense than the current Middle East war-driven episode.
insights.speaker: ECB Blog
insights.so_what: A two-standard-deviation gap is a large, quantifiable signal that the current inflation scare is structurally smaller than 2022, arguing against pricing in 2022-style aggressive ECB tightening.
insights.quote: business price expectations stood significantly above their current level – by about two standard deviations
insights.locator: After Russia's invasion of Ukraine, business price expectations stood significantly above their current level

insights.claim: In 2022, demand-pull pressures dominated (buoyant post-pandemic reopening demand, especially in services) combined with supply constrained by global manufacturing bottlenecks, whereas in 2026 cost-push forces from energy have played the comparatively larger role with demand staying flat — a materially different shock composition despite superficially similar energy-price triggers.
insights.speaker: ECB Blog
insights.so_what: Against a naive assumption that 'another war, another oil shock' means 'another 2022,' the data show this episode is a narrower, single-cause (energy) shock without the demand overhang — a reason to expect less persistent inflation and a more measured ECB response.
insights.quote: Demand-pull pressures dominated in 2022, whereas cost-push inflationary forces have played a comparatively larger role in the current episode.
insights.locator: As these findings reveal, today's picture is quite different from the one in 2022.

insights.claim: Because the current inflation rise is judged to be first and foremost a supply shock rather than a broad-based demand surge, it does not automatically call for the same forceful monetary tightening that a demand-pull episode like 2022 would warrant.
insights.speaker: ECB Blog
insights.so_what: This is the article's core policy takeaway: markets should not expect the ECB to respond to the current energy-driven inflation uptick with 2022-style aggressive rate hikes.
insights.quote: A supply-driven inflation episode does not automatically call for the same forceful tightening that demand-pull inflation would warrant.
insights.locator: For the ECB, these findings matter.

insights.claim: Supply shocks can still become entrenched and warrant a policy response if they feed more broadly into wages or inflation expectations and add to demand pressures, so the ECB needs to keep monitoring second-round effects even while treating this as primarily a supply shock.
insights.speaker: ECB Blog
insights.so_what: The key risk to watch is wage-price second-round effects from the energy shock; if wage growth or inflation expectations start moving with the energy narrative, the ECB's calculus shifts toward tightening.
insights.quote: supply shocks can become entrenched if they feed more broadly into wages or inflation expectations and add to demand pressures
insights.locator: However, supply shocks can become entrenched

insights.claim: The authors position combining earnings-call/press textual analysis with business-survey structural decomposition as an early-warning system that lets the ECB read the demand/supply drivers of inflation ahead of official hard data, to calibrate policy more accurately in real time.
insights.speaker: ECB Blog
insights.so_what: This signals the ECB's own analytical toolkit is shifting toward NLP/text-based nowcasting; investors tracking ECB reaction functions should watch these same forward-looking proxies rather than waiting for lagging hard data.
insights.quote: Combined, they provide an early-warning system – grounded in what newspapers report, as well as in what firms say and expect – that can help central banks stay ahead of rapidly shifting economic conditions.
insights.locator: Monitoring the drivers of inflation based on firms' expectations
